questions.question: The 50/30/20 rule splits take-home pay into…
questions.explanation: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings or debt repayment.

questions.question: On £2,000 take-home a month, how much does 50/30/20 say to save?
Which of these is a “need”?
questions.explanation: Needs are essentials such as housing, bills and food.

questions.question: “Pay yourself first” means…
options: Move money to savings as soon as you're paid, before spending
questions.explanation: Saving first means it actually happens.

questions.question: A forgotten £12.99-a-month subscription costs you how much a year?
The quickest way to find forgotten subscriptions is…
options: Check your bank app for recurring payments
questions.explanation: Most banking apps list recurring payments.

questions.question: Saving £5 a day adds up to roughly how much a year?
A sinking fund is…
options: Money saved bit by bit for a known future cost, like an MOT or Christmas
questions.explanation: Sinking funds stop predictable costs becoming surprises.

questions.question: Which is a SMART goal?
options: “Save £600 for a holiday by June by putting away £100 a month”
questions.explanation: It's specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

questions.question: If you spend more than you earn, you have…
questions.explanation: A deficit means money is running out or debt is building.

questions.question: Zero-based budgeting means…
options: Giving every pound of income a job until nothing is unassigned
questions.explanation: Every pound is planned, including savings.

questions.question: Take-home pay £2,200. Rent £900, bills £250, food £300, transport £150. What share goes on these needs?
A good trick against impulse buying is…
options: Buying immediately before the price rises
questions.explanation: A pause lets the urge pass.

questions.question: “Lifestyle creep” is when…
options: Spending rises with your income, so you don't save more
A scam slowly drains your account
questions.explanation: Save part of every pay rise before you get used to it.

questions.question: Which of these is usually a fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Fixed costs stay the same each month. Variable costs change.

questions.question: Your car insurance costs £600 once a year. The best way to handle it is…
options: Put it on a credit card when it's due
questions.explanation: Saving monthly for yearly costs (a sinking fund) stops them becoming a shock.

questions.question: Envelope (or “pots”) budgeting means…
options: Splitting money into separate pots for each type of spending
Paying in cash once a year
questions.explanation: Many banking apps let you create pots to do this digitally.

questions.question: You want £6,000 saved in 2 years. How much do you need to save each month?
Tracking every penny you spend for a month mainly helps you…
options: See where your money actually goes
questions.explanation: Most people underestimate small, frequent spending.

questions.question: You have several debts and a bit of spare money. A sensible first step is…
options: Check which debt costs the most interest
questions.explanation: Knowing your interest rates tells you which debt costs you the most.

questions.question: The “debt snowball” method means…
options: Paying off the smallest balance first for quick wins
questions.explanation: Snowball builds motivation. “Avalanche” (highest rate first) usually saves more interest.

questions.question: Card A: £500 at 30%. Card B: £2,000 at 20%. You have £100 a month extra. The “avalanche” method puts it on…
questions.explanation: Avalanche targets the highest interest rate first (while paying minimums on the rest).

questions.question: Your “take-home pay” is…
options: Your pay after tax, National Insurance and other deductions
questions.explanation: Budget with take-home pay, not your headline salary.

questions.question: A £1,000 sofa on “0% interest for 12 months” is only the cheap option if…
options: You clear it before the deal ends
questions.explanation: After the 0% ends, interest can be high. Some deals backdate interest if not cleared.

questions.question: A budget should be…
questions.explanation: Life changes, so your budget should too.

questions.question: Where can you get free, impartial debt advice in the UK?
options: Charities such as StepChange or Citizens Advice, or MoneyHelper
questions.explanation: Free debt advice is available. You never need to pay for it.
